title: Why give before you ask?
principle: A real gift, given first, makes people want to give back.

screens.text: Let me tell you about a test in an American restaurant. When waiters brought the bill, some gave no sweet at all, some put one chocolate on the bill, and some put two. And some did something a little different. Let me show you.

screens.prompt: In the last group, the waiter gave one chocolate, walked away, then turned back and gave a second, "just for you". Which group tipped most?

options.label: One, then a second on turning back

screens.why: Compared with no chocolate, one chocolate raised tips by about 3%. Two raised them by about 14%. But one, then a second "just for you", raised them by about 21%.

screens.title: Reciprocity
screens.text: This is called reciprocity. When someone gives us something first, we feel we owe them, and we want to give back. Robert Cialdini wrote about it in his book Influence. And look at the chocolates again: how a gift is given matters as much as the gift.

screens.title: It's used on you
screens.text: You'll see this everywhere. The free first class a tuition teacher gives. The extra laddoo the sweet shop drops into your box. The cup of chai a saree shop serves you before you start to bargain. Each one makes you feel you owe something back.

screens.prompt: A jeweller cleans your old chain for free while you wait. Then he shows you new chains. You feel bad leaving without buying. Why?

options.label: The new chains were better than you expected
Waiting there made you stay much longer
He did something for you first

screens.why: Yes. He gave first, so leaving with nothing feels like not paying back. That's reciprocity at work on you.

wrong.a: Maybe, but you'd feel bad leaving even if they were ordinary. He cleaned your chain for free first, so you feel you owe him.
wrong.b: A longer visit adds a little. But even a short visit with a free cleaning leaves you feeling you owe him. The gift came first.

screens.title: Where it goes wrong
screens.text: Reciprocity can backfire. A tiny gift, like a crumb, feels cheap. A gift with a hook, like "free, if you order now", feels like a deal, so nobody feels they owe you. And a costly gift to one person, just before you ask for an order, feels like a bribe.

screens.title: Now look at your business
screens.text: A restaurant in America and your bakery seem far apart, but people feel the same pull everywhere. It's mid-September. Your housing society holds a ten-day Ganesh festival. About 200 families come each evening, and you can set up a small table.

screens.prompt: On the first evening, you can spend ₹2,000 on free tasting. Which gift will bring you the most orders?

options.label: Small crumbs on toothpicks for all 200 families
A full cupcake each for 50 families
A free cupcake with every cake ordered that day

screens.why: Exactly. A full cupcake feels like a real gift, so people want to give back. A crumb feels cheap, and a gift that needs an order isn't a gift.

wrong.a: More people taste, but a crumb on a toothpick feels cheap. A gift must feel real before people want to give back. 50 full cupcakes beat 200 crumbs.
wrong.c: That's a deal, not a gift. It asks for an order first, so nobody feels they owe you. Give first, with nothing asked.

screens.prompt: Let's check it. 50 free cupcakes cost you ₹40 each. 8 families then order an ₹850 cake, and each leaves you ₹450. What's left?
screens.why: Well done. 8 cakes × ₹450 = ₹3,600. The cupcakes cost 50 × ₹40 = ₹2,000. So ₹1,600 is left, and those 8 families can order again for every birthday.

wrong.b: I see what you did: 8 × ₹450 = ₹3,600. But the 50 cupcakes cost you ₹2,000. Take that away: ₹1,600 is left.
wrong.c: You used the price, ₹850, not the ₹450 you keep. 8 × ₹450 = ₹3,600, minus ₹2,000 for the cupcakes, leaves ₹1,600.

screens.prompt: I'll show you six things a baker might give. For each one, tell me: is it a real gift, or a gift with a hook?

items.text: A full cupcake, with nothing asked
A free cupcake if you share our post with 10 friends
A card with an easy eggless cookie recipe
A "free" cake that comes with a ₹2,000 order
An extra cookie in the box, with a thank-you note
A free taste, then a push to order on the spot

screens.why: A real gift asks for nothing back. Once a gift needs a share, an order or a quick "yes", it feels like a deal, and nobody feels they owe you.

screens.setup: It's the end of September. A big office down the road has never ordered from you. Diwali is a month away, and offices buy gift boxes then. Your ₹500 Diwali box costs ₹300 to make. You have ₹3,000 to spend winning them.
screens.question: What do you do?

options.label: Send the manager a ₹3,000 gift, hoping for an order
options.outcome: The manager feels uneasy. A costly gift to one person, just before Diwali orders, looks like a bribe. She returns it politely and orders elsewhere. You've lost ₹3,000.
options.why: A gift to one decision-maker, timed for an order, has a hook. It makes people feel bought, not thankful.
options.better: Send cupcakes for the whole team, with a note and no ask.

options.label: Offer ₹50 off each box if they order this week
options.outcome: The manager orders 20 boxes at ₹450. Each leaves you ₹150: ₹3,000 in all. The staff never taste your baking, so nobody asks for you next year.
options.why: A discount is a deal, not a gift. It won a small order, but nobody felt they owed you anything.
options.better: Send cupcakes for the whole team, with a note and no ask.

options.label: Send 60 cupcakes for the staff, with a note
options.outcome: The cupcakes cost you ₹2,400. The staff love them. A week later, the manager calls and orders 60 Diwali boxes at ₹500. Each leaves you ₹200: ₹12,000. After the cupcakes, ₹9,600 is left.
options.why: A real gift to the whole team, with nothing asked, made them want to give back.

screens.title: The honest line
screens.text: Here's a line to keep for this whole unit: use on others only what you'd accept being used on you. Your cupcakes are fair: nothing asked, no pressure, and buying stays their choice. Chai served only to make people feel bad leaving is not.
Give a ___ gift ___, and people want to give back.
screens.why: Exactly. The waiter's second chocolate felt real and personal. Full cupcakes for a whole team, with nothing asked, work the same way. Give first, ask later.

summary: Reciprocity: when someone gives us something first, we want to give back.
A real gift works. Crumbs feel cheap, and a gift with a hook is a deal, not a gift.
Give to the whole team, with nothing asked. A costly gift to one person to win an order looks like a bribe.

cards.front: A sweet shop wants tasters to buy. What should it hand out?
cards.back: A real gift makes people want to give back. Crumbs feel cheap.

cards.front: "Free cupcake if you share our post with 10 friends." What is it?
cards.back: A gift that asks for something back is a deal. Nobody feels they owe you.

cards.front: You want a big office's Diwali order. Which gift is fair?
options: A costly gift to the manager
Cupcakes for the whole team, no ask
cards.back: Give to the team, with nothing asked. A costly gift to one person feels like a bribe.

sources.label: Strohmetz, Rind, Fisher and Lynn, Sweetening the Till (Journal of Applied Social Psychology, 2002), study 2 figures
